title: Setting the Mood
objectives: I can explain the difference between mood and atmosphere.
I can name the details an author uses to create a feeling.
I can use mood words to describe a place in my own writing.
I can use context clues to understand a feeling word in a story.
rationale: Students need precise words to describe how a text feels and to prove it with details. The ten words begin with the two craft terms, mood and atmosphere, then split into scary or uneasy words, sad or empty words, and joyful or peaceful words. The passage changes mood four times so students can see setting details at work. The unit builds on the figurative-language tools from unit 6 by showing why a detail carries feeling.

passage.title: The Walk to the Old Farm
paras: On the first night of the harvest fair, the whole town felt festive. Lanterns hung over the square, a band played, and Ana's little brother ran past with a candy apple in each hand. But Grandpa had asked Ana to carry a jar of honey to Mr. Reyes at the old farm before dark, and she wished she could stay at the fair.

Past the last streetlight, the road grew desolate. No houses stood on either side, only a few bare trees. The sky turned an ominous gray, and wind pushed dry leaves across the path. An eerie fog rose from the ditch, and Ana walked faster.

At the farm, the yard looked bleak, with frozen mud and a broken fence. Ana felt tense, and every creak of the gate seemed loud. Then the door opened. Mr. Reyes spoke in a somber voice. "This is my last season here," he said. "I am moving to the city." He led her into the kitchen, where a kettle hummed and the stove glowed. The room was serene, and Ana's fear faded.

Walking home with a thank-you card in her pocket, Ana thought about her writing notebook. A good writer controls the mood, she realized. The atmosphere of her walk had changed four times: festive, eerie, sad, and calm. She could not wait to write it down.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "desolate" most nearly means
qs.why: No houses, only a few bare trees: the road has no people or life, so desolate means empty and lonely.

qs.q: Why does Ana walk faster in paragraph 2?
choices: She is late for the fair.
She wants to race the wind.
She is excited to see Mr. Reyes.
The fog and gray sky make the road feel frightening.
qs.why: The ominous sky and eerie fog create a scary atmosphere, so she hurries.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the farm yard feels bleak?
choices: Frozen mud and a broken fence
A kettle humming on the stove
Ana carrying a jar of honey
qs.why: Frozen mud and a broken fence are cold, dull, and uncomfortable details.

qs.q: What does Mr. Reyes's somber voice suggest?
choices: He is sad about leaving the farm.
He is tired from the fair.
qs.why: He says it is his last season and he is moving, so somber shows serious sadness.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Mr. Reyes is moving and Ana is angry.
Fairs are always more fun than farms.
The mood of a walk can change as the setting and details change.
Fog on a road is dangerous at night.
qs.why: The passage moves from festive to eerie to sad to calm, and says the atmosphere changed four times.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for mood and atmosphere, trace how a narrative's setting details change its feeling, and write scenes that build a mood on purpose. The unit uses the figurative-language tools from unit 6 to explain why a detail creates a feeling.

notes.va.mood.n: Mood is the feeling the reader gets; atmosphere is the feeling of the place. Mood can also mean a person's own feeling, which is a different use in everyday speech. Use a two-column chart.
notes.va.atmosphere.n: Atmosphere has a science sense (air around a planet) and a literary sense. Teach the literary sense first and note the shared idea of surrounding something.
notes.va.ominous.adj: Ominous works as a warning. Ask what bad thing the reader expects. Practice with weather and sound details, and connect to symbolize from unit 6.
notes.va.serene.adj: Serene is peaceful in a deep way. Students may confuse it with quiet; a place can be quiet and still be eerie.
notes.va.eerie.adj: Eerie is strange and a little scary. Many students will say scary for everything, so have them sort scary details into eerie and ominous.
notes.va.somber.adj: Somber is serious sadness or a dark tone. It is not a loud sadness. Show a gray painting or a quiet ceremony.
notes.va.desolate.adj: Desolate is empty and lonely. Compare with bleak: desolate is about what a place lacks, bleak is about cold, hopeless feeling.
notes.va.bleak.adj: Bleak applies to places and to futures. Link to associate from unit 6: ask which colors and weather students associate with bleak.
notes.va.festive.adj: Festive is positive and connected to festivals, which students can use as a clue. Have them build a festive and a desolate scene from the same location.
notes.va.tense.adj: Tense also names a verb form. Reassure students that the two meanings are unrelated in use, and ask which meaning a sentence needs.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The author says the road grew desolate, the sky turned ominous, and a fog was eerie. All three details are scary or lonely. So the mood is uneasy. When I describe it, I will name the details that made me feel that way.'
discuss: Which book have you read with a strong atmosphere? Which details created it?
Can a place be both festive and tense? Explain.
misconceptions: Mood and atmosphere are exactly the same.
Eerie and ominous mean the same thing.
Tense only means a verb form.

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit onomatopoeia, symbolize, and associate by asking students to find one in a scene and say how it supports the mood. Return to the mood ladders after two days and again at one week.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (ambiente emocional, ambiente, inquietante, desolador) not reviewed by a native speaker; mood has no single Spanish equivalent for the literary sense.
Sense boundary of mood versus atmosphere versus tone: teachers sometimes use them loosely; the unit treats mood as the reader's feeling and atmosphere as the feeling of the place.
Origin of omen/ominous noted only as a spelling change; no etymology claim made.
